summary: Defines MIB objects for managing the fourth version of BGP using SMIv2. It was a draft standard. It was replaced by RFC 4273.

eli5.summary: Gauges for checking how a BGP router is doing. A newer version replaced it.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for BGP-4 routers.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standardized way to monitor and manage Border Gateway Protocol version 4 routers using SNMP, the standard network management protocol.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1657 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with SNMP objects to track BGP peer connections, routes, and statistics.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was superseded by RFC 4273, which provides updated management definitions for modern BGP deployments.

today: RFC 1657 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4273, which provides updated MIB definitions for BGP-4. The newer RFC adds support for additional BGP extensions and attributes that emerged after 1994.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1657 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) for SNMP network management of Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4) implementations. The MIB allows network operators to monitor and control BGP routers using the same SNMP protocol framework used for other network devices.

The RFC integrates with the SNMPv2 framework, building on the SMI (Structure of Management Information) standard to describe how BGP operational data is exposed to management systems.
sections.eli5: Think of this as a way to peek inside a BGP router and see what it is doing, using the same language network managers use to check on other network equipment.

sections.title: BGP MIB Structure
sections.content:
The BGP-4 MIB defines three main tables and several scalar objects. The BGP Peer Table contains an entry for each peer connection with detailed state and activity information. The Received Path Attribute Table (deprecated) held attributes from BGP-3 peers. The BGP-4 Received Path Attribute Table holds current path attributes received from BGP-4 peers.

System-wide objects include the BGP identifier and the local autonomous system number. Administrators can control BGP peer connections by setting the peer administrative status (start or stop).
sections.eli5: The MIB is organized like a file cabinet: one drawer for peer connections, one for the paths BGP learned, and separate slots for system settings.

sections.title: BGP Peer Connection Monitoring
sections.content:
The Peer Table tracks each BGP neighbor connection with fields for connection state, local and remote IP addresses, port numbers, and the remote autonomous system number. The connection state has six values: idle, connect, active, opensent, openconfirm, and established.

The table captures operational metrics such as the count of UPDATE messages sent and received, total message counts, and the time since the last UPDATE arrived. Timers like Hold Time and Keep-Alive are also exposed, both as configured values and negotiated with the peer.
sections.eli5: For each peer, the MIB tracks whether the connection is up or down, how many messages have been exchanged, and how long it has been since the peer sent anything.

sections.title: Path Attributes and Routes
sections.content:
Path attributes describe the characteristics of routes learned from peers. Each path attribute entry records the peer address, the destination network prefix and its length, the origin of the path (IGP, EGP, or incomplete), and the AS path segment sequence.

Additional attributes include the next hop address, the multi-exit discriminator metric, local preference, whether the route is atomic aggregate, and any aggregator information. The MIB also tracks whether this route was selected as the best route and any unknown attributes not recognized by the router.
sections.eli5: For each route the router learned, these fields say which peer told us about it, where it leads, and how good a choice it is compared to other routes.

sections.title: Configuration and Timers
sections.content:
The MIB exposes multiple timer values that control BGP behavior. The Hold Time is negotiated during peer setup with a minimum of 3 seconds if used; the suggested value is 90 seconds. The Keep-Alive timer determines KEEPALIVE message frequency, typically one third of the Hold Time (suggested 30 seconds).

The ConnectRetry interval controls reconnection attempts (suggested 120 seconds). The MinASOriginationInterval (suggested 15 seconds) and MinRouteAdvertisementInterval (suggested 30 seconds) govern how often route updates are sent to peers.
sections.eli5: These timers are like the rhythm of a conversation: how long to wait before giving up, when to say hello to keep the connection alive, and how fast to announce new routes.

sections.title: Notifications and Status
sections.content:
The MIB defines two SNMP notification (trap) types. The bgpEstablished notification is sent when a BGP peer connection reaches the ESTABLISHED state. The bgpBackwardTransition notification is sent when the connection moves to a lower-numbered state (indicating a failure or reset).

These notifications let network management systems monitor BGP stability in real time, alerting operators immediately when peers go down or come back up.
sections.eli5: When important BGP events happen, like a peer connection coming up or going down, the router sends an alert to the management system.
